n:
*Study note:* *Psalm 91*. In this psalm an individual (perhaps a priest) addresses one who has sought shelter in the Lord and assures him that God will protect him from danger (vv. 1-13). In vv. 14-16 God himself promises to keep his loyal follower safe.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[O] one who lives.”

*Study note:* The divine title “Most High” (עֶלְיוֹן ʿelyon) pictures God as the exalted ruler of the universe who vindicates the innocent and judges the wicked. See especially {{Psalm 7:17|Pss 7:17}}; {{Psalm 9:2|9:2}}; {{Psalm 18:13|18:13}}; {{Psalm 21:7|21:7}}; {{Psalm 47:2|47:2}}.

*Study note:* The Lord is compared here to a bird who protects its young under the *shadow* of its wings (see v. {{Psalm 91:4|4}}).

*Study note:* The divine name used here is “Shaddai” (שַׁדַּי, shadday; see also {{Psalm 68:14|Ps 68:14}}). Shaddai (or El Shaddai) is the Sovereign God of the world who grants life/blesses and kills/judges. In Genesis he blesses the patriarchs with fertility and promises numerous descendants. Outside Genesis he both blesses/protects and takes away life/happiness.
*Translator's note:* The word refers specifically to a fowler (or hunter of birds).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “put a cover over you” (see {{Psalm 5:11|Ps 5:11}}).

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text has the singular, but the plural should be read. The final י (yod) of the suffix, which indicates the plural, has dropped off by haplography (note the *yod* at the beginning of the next word).

*Translator's note:* Traditionally the Hebrew term סֹחֵרָה (sokherah), which occurs only here in the OT, has been understood to refer to a buckler or small shield (see BDB 695 s.v.). But *HALOT* 750 s.v., on the basis of evidence from the cognate languages, proposes the meaning “wall.”
*Translator's note:* This probably alludes to a sneak attack by enemies in the darkness of night (see Song 3:8).

*Study note:* As in {{Deuteronomy 32:23|Deut 32:23-24}}, vv. {{Psalm 91:5|5-6}} closely associate military attack and deadly disease. Perhaps the latter alludes to one of the effects of siege warfare on the population of an entrapped city, which was especially vulnerable to the outbreak of epidemics.
*Translator's note:* Apparently the deadly disease mentioned in v. {{Psalm 91:6|6b}} is the understood subject here.

*Translator's note:* Or “confront.”

*Translator's note:* For this sense of the Hebrew term נגע see {{Psalm 38:11|Ps 38:11}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your tent.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for his angels he will command concerning you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in all your ways.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so your foot will not strike a stone.”

*Translator's note:* The words “the Lord says” are supplied in the translation to clarify that the words which follow are the Lord’s oracle of assurance.

*Translator's note:* Or “make him secure” (*Heb* “set him on high”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “because he knows my name” (see {{Psalm 9:10|Ps 9:10}}).

*Study note:* *Psalm 92*. The psalmist praises God because he defeats the wicked and vindicates his loyal followers.

*Translator's note:* Or “good.”

*Study note:* The divine title “Most High” (עֶלְיוֹן ʿelyon) pictures God as the exalted ruler of the universe who vindicates the innocent and judges the wicked. See especially {{Psalm 7:17|Pss 7:17}}; {{Psalm 9:2|9:2}}; {{Psalm 18:13|18:13}}; {{Psalm 21:7|21:7}}; {{Psalm 47:2|47:2}}.

*Translator's note:* The words “it is fitting” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons. Verses {{Psalm 92:1|1-3}} are actually one long sentence in the Hebrew text, but this has been divided up into two shorter sentences in the translation in keeping with contemporary English style.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “very deep [are] your thoughts.” God’s “thoughts” refer here to his moral design of the world, as outlined in vv. {{Psalm 92:6|6-15}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the brutish man does not know, and the fool does not understand this.” The adjective בַּעַר (baʿar, “brutish”) refers to spiritual insensitivity, not mere lack of intelligence or reasoning ability (see {{Psalm 49:10|Pss 49:10}}; {{Psalm 73:22|73:22}}; {{Proverbs 12:1|Prov 12:1}}; {{Proverbs 30:2|30:2}}, as well as the use of the related verb in {{Psalm 94:8|Ps 94:8}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “flourish.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in order that they might be destroyed permanently.”

*Study note:* God allows the wicked to prosper temporarily so that he might reveal his justice. When the wicked are *annihilated*, God demonstrates that wickedness does not pay off.

*Study note:* The *horn* of the *wild ox* is frequently a metaphor for military strength; the idiom “to exalt/lift up the horn” signifies military victory (see {{1 Samuel 2:10|1 Sam 2:10}}; {{Psalm 75:10|Pss 75:10}}; {{Psalm 89:24|89:24}}; Lam 2:17).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb בָּלַל (balal) usually has the nuance “to mix.” Here it seems to mean “to smear” or “to anoint.” Some emend the form to בַּלֹּתַנִי (ballotani; a second person form of the verb with a first person suffix) and read, “you anoint me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my eye gazes upon my walls.” See also {{Psalm 5:8|Pss 5:8}}; {{Psalm 27:11|27:11}}; {{Psalm 56:2|56:2}}. The form שׁוּרָי shuray, “my walls”) should be emended to שׁוֹרְרָי (shoreray, “my foes” or perhaps “those who rebel against me” or “those who malign me”). See *HALOT* 1454 s.v. שׁוֹרֵר and also {{Psalm 5:8|Pss 5:8}}; {{Psalm 27:11|27:11}}; {{Psalm 56:2|56:2}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who rise up against me, evil [foes], my ears hear.”

*Translator's note:* The singular is used in a representative sense, with the typical godly person being in view.

*Study note:* The cedars of the Lebanon forest were well-known in ancient Israel for their immense size.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “so that [they] proclaim that upright [is] the Lord, my rocky summit, and there is no injustice in him.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 93*. The psalmist affirms that the Lord is the king of the universe who preserves order and suppresses the destructive forces in the world.

*Study note:* *Strength* is compared here to a belt that one wears for support. The Lord’s power undergirds his rule.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from antiquity [are] you.” As the context suggests, this refers specifically to God’s royal position, not his personal existence.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun translated “waves” often refers to rivers or streams, but here it appears to refer to the surging waves of the sea (see v. {{Psalm 93:4|4}}, {{Psalm 24:2|Ps 24:2}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the waves lift up, O Lord, the waves lift up their voice, the waves lift up their crashing.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “mighty waters.”

*Study note:* The *surging waters* here symbolizes the hostile enemies of God who seek to destroy the order he has established in the world (see {{Psalm 18:17|Pss 18:17}}; {{Psalm 29:3|29:3}}; {{Psalm 32:6|32:6}}; {{Psalm 77:20|77:20}}; {{Psalm 144:7|144:7}}; {{Isaiah 17:13|Isa 17:13}}; Jer 51:55; {{Ezekiel 26:19|Ezek 26:19}}; {{Habakkuk 3:15|Hab 3:15}}). But the Lord is depicted as elevated above and sovereign over these raging waters.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “mighty on high [is] the Lord.”

*Translator's note:* Traditionally “your testimonies.” The Hebrew noun עֵדוּת (ʿedut) refers here to the demands of God’s covenant law. See {{Psalm 19:7|Ps 19:7}}.

*Study note:* *The rules you set down*. God’s covenant contains a clear, reliable witness to his moral character and demands.

*Study note:* *Holiness* refers here to God’s royal transcendence (see vv. {{Psalm 93:1|1-4}}), as well as his moral authority and perfection (see v. {{Psalm 93:5|5a}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for your house holiness is fitting, O Lord, for length of days.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 94*. The psalmist asks God to judge the wicked and affirms his confidence in God’s justice.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “shine forth” (see {{Psalm 50:2|Pss 50:2}}; {{Psalm 80:1|80:1}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they gush forth [words].”

*Translator's note:* The Hitpael of אָמַר (ʾamar) occurs only here (and perhaps in {{Isaiah 61:6|Isa 61:6}}).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun יָתוֹם (yatom) refers to one who has lost his father (not necessarily his mother, see {{Psalm 109:9|Ps 109:9}}). Because they were so vulnerable and were frequently exploited, fatherless children are often mentioned as epitomizing the oppressed (see {{Psalm 10:14|Pss 10:14}}; {{Psalm 68:5|68:5}}; {{Psalm 82:3|82:3}}; {{Psalm 146:9|146:9}}; as well as {{Job 6:27|Job 6:27}}; {{Job 22:9|22:9}}; {{Job 24:3|24:3}}, {{Job 24:9|9}}; {{Job 29:12|29:12}}; {{Job 31:17|31:17}}, {{Job 31:21|21}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “understand.” The verb used in v. {{Psalm 94:7|7}} is repeated here for rhetorical effect. The people referred to here claim God is ignorant of their actions, but the psalmist corrects their faulty viewpoint.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[you] brutish among the people.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “The one who plants an ear, does he not hear? The one who forms an eye, does he not see?”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord knows the thoughts of man, that they are emptiness.” The psalmist thinks specifically of the “thoughts” expressed in v. {{Psalm 94:7|7}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[Oh] the happiness [of] the man.” Hebrew wisdom literature often assumes and reflects the male-oriented perspective of ancient Israelite society. The principle of the psalm is certainly applicable to all people, regardless of their gender or age. To facilitate modern application, we translate the gender and age specific “man” with the more neutral “one.” The generic masculine pronoun is used in v. {{Psalm 94:2|2}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to give him rest from the days of trouble.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “until a pit is dug for the wicked.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for judgment will return to justice.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the pure of heart.” The “heart” is here viewed as the seat of one’s moral character and motives. The “pure of heart” are God’s faithful followers who trust in and love the Lord and, as a result, experience his deliverance (see {{Psalm 7:10|Pss 7:10}}; {{Psalm 11:2|11:2}}; {{Psalm 32:11|32:11}}; {{Psalm 36:10|36:10}}; {{Psalm 64:10|64:10}}; {{Psalm 97:11|97:11}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and after it [are] the pure of heart.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for me.”

*Study note:* *Who will stand up for me…?* The questions anticipate the answer, “No one except God” (see v. {{Psalm 94:17|17}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “If the Lord [were] not my help, quickly my life would have dwelt in silence.” The psalmist, perhaps speaking as the nation’s representative, recalls God’s past intervention. For other examples of conditional sentences with the term לוּלֵי (lule, “if not”) in the protasis and a perfect verbal form in the apodosis, see {{Psalm 119:92|Pss 119:92}} and {{Psalm 124:2|124:2-5}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when my worries are many within me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your comforts cause my soul to delight.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a throne of destruction.” “Throne” stands here by metonymy for rulers who occupy thrones.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Is a throne of destruction united to you, one that forms trouble upon a statute?” The rhetorical question anticipates the answer, “Of course not!” The translation, while not preserving the interrogative form of the statement, reflects its rhetorical force.

*Translator's note:* Or “attack.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the life of the blameless.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the blood of the innocent they declare guilty.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the Lord has become my elevated place.” The prefixed verbal form with vav (ו) consecutive is used in a rhetorical sense, describing an anticipated development as if it were already reality.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my God [has become] a rocky summit of my safety.”

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form with vav (ו) consecutive is used in a rhetorical sense, describing an anticipated development as if it were already reality.

*Translator's note:* Or “in.”

*Study note:* *Psalm 95*. The psalmist summons Israel to praise God as the creator of the world and the nation’s protector, but he also reminds the people not to rebel against God.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to the rocky summit of our deliverance.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “meet his face.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with songs of joy.”
*Translator's note:* The phrase “in his hand” means within the sphere of his authority.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “of his hand.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “if only you would listen to his voice.” The Hebrew particle אִם (ʾim, “if”) and following prefixed verbal form here express a wish (cf. {{Psalm 81:8|Ps 81:8}}). Note that the apodosis (the “then” clause of the conditional sentence) is suppressed.

*Translator's note:* The words “he says” are supplied in the translation to clarify that the following words are spoken by the Lord (see vv. {{Psalm 95:9|9-11}}).

*Study note:* The name *Meribah* means “strife.” Two separate but similar incidents at Meribah are recorded in the Pentateuch ({{Exodus 17:1|Exod 17:1-7}}; {{Numbers 20:1|Num 20:1-13}}, see also {{Psalm 81:7|Pss 81:7}}; {{Psalm 106:32|106:32}}). In both cases the Israelites complained about lack of water and the Lord miraculously provided for them.

*Study note:* The name *Massah* means “testing.” This was another name (along with Meribah) given to the place where Israel complained following the Red Sea Crossing (see {{Exodus 17:1|Exod 17:1-7}}, as well as {{Deuteronomy 6:16|Deut 6:16}}; {{Deuteronomy 9:22|9:22}}; {{Deuteronomy 33:8|33:8}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not harden your heart[s] as [at] Meribah, as [in] the day of Massah in the wilderness.”

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal form is either a preterite or an imperfect. If the latter, it emphasizes the ongoing nature of the condition in the past. The translation reflects this interpretation of the verbal form.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a people, wanderers of heart [are] they.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they do not know my ways.” In this context the Lord’s “ways” are his commands, viewed as a pathway from which his people, likened to wayward sheep (see v. {{Psalm 95:7|7}}), wander.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my resting place.” The promised land of Canaan is here viewed metaphorically as a place of rest for God’s people, who are compared to sheep (see v. {{Psalm 95:7|7}}).

*Study note:* *Psalm 96*. The psalmist summons everyone to praise the Lord, the sovereign creator of the world who preserves and promotes justice in the earth.

*Study note:* A *new song* is appropriate because the Lord is constantly intervening in the world as its just king. See also {{Psalm 33:3|Pss 33:3}}; {{Psalm 40:3|40:3}}; {{Psalm 98:1|98:1}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “announce from day to day his deliverance.”
*Translator's note:* The verb “tell” is understood by ellipsis (note the preceding line).
*Translator's note:* Or perhaps “and feared by all gods.” See {{Psalm 89:7|Ps 89:7}}.
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term אֱלִילִים (ʾelilim, “worthless”) sounds like אֱלֹהִים (ʾelohim, “gods”). The sound play draws attention to the statement.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “majesty and splendor [are] before him.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “strength and beauty [are] in his sanctuary.”

*Translator's note:* The verbal forms in v. {{Psalm 96:13|13}} probably describe God’s typical, characteristic behavior, though they may depict in dramatic fashion the outworking of divine judgment or anticipate a future judgment of worldwide proportions, in which case they could be translated “will judge the world.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the nations with his integrity.”
*Study note:* *Psalm 97*. The psalmist depicts the Lord as the sovereign, just king of the world who comes in power to vindicate his people.
*Study note:* The Lord’s *throne* symbolizes his kingship.

*Translator's note:* The translation assumes that the prefixed verbal form in the first line is an imperfect (“are ashamed”) and that the ambiguous form in the third line is a perfect (“bow down”) because the psalmist appears to be describing the effect of the Lord’s mighty theophany on those who witness it (see vv. {{Psalm 97:5|5}}, {{Psalm 97:8|8}}). Another option is to take the prefixed form in the first line as a jussive (“let all who worship idols be ashamed”) and the ambiguous form in the third line as an imperative (“All you gods, bow down before him!”; cf. NIV).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “daughters.” The term “daughters” refers to the cities of Judah surrounding Zion (see {{Psalm 48:11|Ps 48:11}} and H. Haag, *TDOT* 2:336).

*Study note:* The divine title “Most High” (עֶלְיוֹן ʿelyon) pictures God as the exalted ruler of the universe who vindicates the innocent and judges the wicked. See especially {{Psalm 7:17|Pss 7:17}}; {{Psalm 9:2|9:2}}; {{Psalm 18:13|18:13}}; {{Psalm 21:7|21:7}}; {{Psalm 47:2|47:2}}.

*Translator's note:* The participle may be verbal, though it might also be understood as substantival and appositional to “the Lord.” In this case one could translate, “Hate evil, you who love the Lord, the one who protects the lives…and delivers them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hand.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Light is planted for the godly, and for the upright of heart joy.” The translation assumes an emendation of זָרַע (zaraʿ, “planted”) to זָרַח (zarakh, “shines”) which collocates more naturally with “light.” “Light” here symbolizes the joy (note the following line) that accompanies deliverance and the outpouring of divine favor.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to his holy remembrance.” The Hebrew noun זָכַר (zakhar, “remembrance”) here refers to the name of the Lord as invoked in liturgy and praise. Cf. {{Psalm 6:5|Pss 6:5}}; {{Psalm 30:4|30:4}}. The Lord’s “name” is “holy” in the sense that it is a reminder of his uniqueness and greatness.

*Study note:* *Psalm 98*. The psalmist summons the whole earth to praise God because he reveals his justice and delivers Israel.

*Study note:* A *new song* is appropriate because the Lord is constantly intervening in the world as its just king. See {{Psalm 96:1|Ps 96:1}}.

*Translator's note:* The perfect verbal forms in vv. {{Psalm 98:1|1-3}} are understood here as describing characteristic divine activities. Another option is to translate them as present perfects, “has performed…has accomplished deliverance, etc.” referring to completed actions that have continuing results.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his right hand delivers for him and his holy arm.” The right hand and arm symbolize his power as a warrior-king (see {{Isaiah 52:10|Isa 52:10}}). His arm is “holy” in the sense that it is in a category of its own; God’s power is incomparable.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he remembers his loyal love and his faithfulness to the house of Israel.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the deliverance of our God,” with “God” being a subjective genitive (= God delivers).

*Translator's note:* The verbal forms in v. {{Psalm 98:9|9}} probably describe God’s typical, characteristic behavior, though they may depict in dramatic fashion the outworking of divine judgment or anticipate a future judgment of worldwide proportions (“will judge…”).

*Study note:* *Psalm 99*. The psalmist celebrates the Lord’s just rule and recalls how he revealed himself to Israel’s leaders.

*Translator's note:* The prefixed verbal forms in v. {{Psalm 99:1|1}} are understood here as indicating the nations’ characteristic response to the reality of the Lord’s kingship. Another option is to take them as jussives: “let the nations tremble…let the earth shake!”

*Study note:* Cherubim are winged angels. As depicted in the OT, they possess both human and animal (lion, ox, and eagle) characteristics (see {{Ezekiel 1:10|Ezek 1:10}}; {{Ezekiel 10:14|10:14}}, {{Ezekiel 10:21|21}}; {{Ezekiel 41:18|41:18}}). They are pictured as winged creatures ({{Exodus 25:20|Exod 25:20}}; {{Exodus 37:9|37:9}}; {{1 Kings 6:24|1 Kgs 6:24-27}}; {{Ezekiel 10:8|Ezek 10:8}}, {{Ezekiel 10:19|19}}) and serve as the very throne of God when the ark of the covenant is in view ({{Psalm 99:1|Ps 99:1}}; see {{Numbers 7:89|Num 7:89}}; {{1 Samuel 4:4|1 Sam 4:4}}; {{2 Samuel 6:2|2 Sam 6:2}}; {{2 Kings 19:15|2 Kgs 19:15}}). The picture of the Lord seated on the cherubim suggests they might be used by him as a vehicle, a function they carry out in {{Ezekiel 1:22|Ezek 1:22-28}} (the “living creatures” mentioned here are identified as cherubim in {{Ezekiel 10:20|Ezek 10:20}}). In {{Psalm 18:10|Ps 18:10}} the image of a cherub serves to personify the wind.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb נוּט (nut) occurs only here in the OT, but the meaning can be determined on the basis of the parallelism with רָגַז (ragaz, “tremble”) and evidence from the cognate languages (see H. R. Cohen, *Biblical Hapax Legomena* [SBLDS], 121).
*Translator's note:* The pronoun refers to the Lord himself (see vv. {{Psalm 99:5|5}}, {{Psalm 99:9|9}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and strength, a king, justice he loves.” The syntax of the Hebrew text is difficult here. The translation assumes that two affirmations are made about the king, the Lord (see v. {{Psalm 99:1|1}}, and {{Psalm 98:6|Ps 98:6}}). The noun עֹז (ʿoz, “strength”) should probably be revocalized as the adjective עַז (ʿaz, “strong”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you establish fairness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “among those who called on his name.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who.” The participle is in apposition to the phrase “those who called on his name” in the preceding line.
*Study note:* *A pillar of cloud*. The psalmist refers to the reality described in {{Exodus 33:9|Exod 33:9-10}}; {{Numbers 12:5|Num 12:5}}; and {{Deuteronomy 31:15|Deut 31:15}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a God of lifting up [i.e., forgiveness] you were to them, and an avenger concerning their deeds.” The present translation reflects the traditional interpretation, which understands the last line as qualifying the preceding one. God forgave Moses and Aaron, but he also disciplined them when they sinned (cf. NIV, NRSV). Another option is to take “their deeds” as referring to harmful deeds directed against Moses and Aaron. In this case the verse may be translated, “and one who avenged attacks against them.” Still another option is to emend the participial form נֹקֵם (noqem, “an avenger”) to נֹקָם (noqam), a rare Qal participial form of נָקַה (naqah, “purify”) with a suffixed pronoun. In this case one could translate, “and one who purified them from their [sinful] deeds” (cf. NEB “and held them innocent”).
*Study note:* *Psalm 100*. The psalmist celebrates the fact that Israel has a special relationship to God and summons worshipers to praise the Lord for his faithfulness.

*Translator's note:* The present translation (like most modern translations) follows the *Qere* (marginal reading), which reads literally, “and to him [are] we.” The *Kethib* (consonantal text) has “and not we.” The suffixed preposition לוֹ (lo, “to him”) was confused aurally with the negative particle לֹא (loʾ, “not”) because the two sound identical.

*Translator's note:* Or “is forever.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and to a generation and a generation [is] his faithfulness.”
